analysis.summary: This master services agreement is one-sided in most of the sections that matter to you: unlimited revisions, uncapped indemnity, ownership on creation rather than on payment, and a two-year non-compete. Twelve clauses are worth a second look — start with the seven marked high.

findings.clauseExcerpt: Contractor shall provide revisions until Client is fully satisfied with the deliverables.
findings.explanation: There’s no limit on revisions and no definition of “satisfied,” so the project can continue indefinitely at the client’s discretion without additional payment.
findings.suggestedChange: Ask for a specific number of revision rounds — two is standard — with additional rounds billed at your hourly rate.

findings.clauseExcerpt: All work product, including preliminary concepts, sketches, and materials created by Contractor prior to the Effective Date, shall become the sole and exclusive property of Client upon creation.
findings.explanation: This hands over work you made before this project existed, and the assignment takes effect the moment you create something rather than when you’re paid — so an unpaid final invoice leaves you with nothing to hold.
findings.suggestedChange: Ask that this cover only deliverables made under this agreement, and that ownership transfer on receipt of final payment. Offer a licence for anything you made beforehand instead of assigning it.

findings.clauseExcerpt: Contractor shall indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Client against any and all claims, damages, and expenses of any kind whatsoever arising from the Services, without limitation as to amount.
findings.explanation: This is an uncapped indemnity — one dispute could cost you far more than the project pays, including claims caused by material the client gave you.
findings.suggestedChange: Ask to cap your total liability at the fees paid under this agreement, and to exclude claims arising from client-supplied content or client instructions.

findings.clauseExcerpt: For a period of twenty-four (24) months following termination, Contractor shall not provide design services to any business operating in the Client’s industry.
findings.explanation: This is a non-compete: two years across an entire industry can remove a large share of the clients you’d normally work for — a real cost, for something you’re not being paid extra to accept.
findings.suggestedChange: Ask to narrow this to a short list of named direct competitors and to shorten it to six months — or to drop it, since you’re a contractor rather than an employee.

findings.clauseExcerpt: Client may terminate this Agreement at any time, for any reason or no reason, upon written notice, and shall have no obligation to pay for work in progress.
findings.explanation: The client can end the project at any point and owe you nothing for work already underway — there is no kill fee, so the whole cost of a cancellation lands on you.
findings.suggestedChange: Ask for 14 days’ notice, payment for all work completed to date, and 25% of the remaining fee if the project is cancelled after it starts.

findings.clauseExcerpt: In the event Client requests reshooting of any footage for reasons other than technical defect, Producer shall reshoot at no additional charge.
findings.explanation: A reshoot means crew, location and equipment all over again. This clause makes that free and unlimited whenever the client changes their mind — the expensive twin of unlimited revisions.
findings.suggestedChange: Ask that free reshoots cover technical defects only, and that reshoots requested for creative reasons be quoted separately at your day rate.

findings.clauseExcerpt: Producer shall pay Client a penalty of five percent (5%) of the total fee for each day of delay in delivery beyond the agreed date.
findings.explanation: 5% a day reaches the entire fee in twenty days, with no cap and no exception for delays the client causes — a week of late feedback from them could still cost you a third of the project.
findings.suggestedChange: Ask to cap the total penalty at 10% of the fee, and to stop the clock for any delay caused by late client feedback, missing assets, or scheduling changes.

findings.clauseExcerpt: Payment shall be due within ninety (90) days of Client’s acceptance of the final deliverables.
findings.explanation: Net-90 is three months of financing the client’s project, and the clock only starts on acceptance — which the client controls and could delay indefinitely.
findings.suggestedChange: Ask for net-14 or net-30 counted from your invoice date, and for deliverables to be treated as accepted if no feedback arrives within five working days.

findings.clauseExcerpt: Producer may not display, reproduce, or reference the work in any portfolio, showreel, or promotional material.
findings.explanation: For a video producer the showreel is how the next job arrives. An absolute ban makes this project invisible in your work, which is a career cost rather than an admin detail.
findings.suggestedChange: Ask for the right to show the finished work after it’s publicly released — or, if the client needs it kept private, a fee that reflects what the silence is worth.

findings.clauseExcerpt: Client shall pay all undisputed invoices within sixty (60) days of receipt.
findings.explanation: Net-60 means financing the client’s project for two months, and “undisputed” lets any disagreement pause the clock on the whole invoice rather than just the disputed part.
findings.suggestedChange: Ask for net-14 or net-30, and for a dispute to pause payment only on the disputed portion of the invoice.

findings.clauseExcerpt: Developer shall not disclose the existence of this engagement, the identity of Client, or the nature of the Services to any third party without Client’s prior written consent.
findings.explanation: There’s no end date and it covers the client’s identity, so as written you couldn’t list them in your portfolio, mention the work to a future client, or put it on your CV.
findings.suggestedChange: Ask for an explicit carve-out allowing you to name the client and describe the work in your portfolio, and for the clause to expire after two or three years.

findings.clauseExcerpt: Contractor shall bear all costs of software, fonts, stock imagery, and other materials required to perform the Services.
findings.explanation: Minor on its own, but licences for fonts and stock imagery on a branding project can run into hundreds of dollars that come straight out of your fee.
findings.suggestedChange: Ask for materials bought specifically for this project to be reimbursed at cost, or add an allowance for them to the fee.

missingClauses: IP transfer isn’t conditional on payment
